props.title: F for Fake
props.initialSlug: Orson Welles' playful meditation on art & deception

sections.content: F for Fake (1973) represents Orson Welles' most experimental and playful work, a meta-documentary that gleefully demolishes the line between truth and illusion. Like his infamous 1938 "War of the Worlds" radio broadcast, Welles delights in misleading his audience - but this time he tells us upfront he'll only tell the truth for one hour. The film weaves together the stories of art forger Elmyr de Hory and fake Howard Hughes biographer Clifford Irving, with Welles himself serving as a mischievous ringmaster who constantly reminds us of his own history of deception in Citizen Kane (1941).

sections.content: The film's revolutionary editing technique, with rapid-fire cuts and overlapping dialogue, influenced generations of filmmakers exploring truth in documentary. The Act of Killing (2012) borrowed Welles' approach of having subjects dramatically reenact their own stories, while Stories We Tell (2012) echoed his use of staged "archival" footage. Even mainstream documentaries like The Kid Stays in the Picture (2002) adopted F for Fake's self-aware commentary on the nature of storytelling.

Beyond its technical innovation, F for Fake sparked a whole subgenre of documentaries about con artists and art forgery. Tim's Vermeer (2013) explores another outsider attempting to crack the code of a master painter, while Art and Craft (2014) sympathetically profiles a prolific art forger who donated his fakes to museums. The film's examination of expertise and authenticity feels especially relevant in our era of deep fakes and digital manipulation. SUBHEAD: The Art of Cinematic Deception

movies.title: Orson Welles: The One-Man Band
movies.slug: Documentary about Welles' unfinished projects, incorporating many clips from F for Fake

sections.content: Welles understood that cinema itself is a form of magic and illusion. His exploration of fakery connects to later films like The Prestige (2006) and Now You See Me (2013), which use magic and misdirection as metaphors for filmmaking. But while those films ultimately reveal their tricks, Welles keeps us guessing until the end, making the audience complicit in their own deception. This influenced meta-horror films like Cabin in the Woods (2012) which similarly break the fourth wall to comment on genre conventions.
